AN ACT to amend chapter 43 of the laws of 2014, amending the vehicle and
traffic law, the public officers law and the general municipal law relating to
photo speed violation monitoring systems in school speed zones in the city of
New York, in relation to the effectiveness thereof; and the vehicle and
traffic law, in relation to establishing photo speed violation monitoring
systems on the long island expressway
items.lawCode: Amd §12, Chap 43 of 2014; amd §1180-c, V & T L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8263

SPONSOR: HAMILTON
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend chapter 43 of the laws of 2014, amend-
ing the vehicle and traffic law, the public officers law and the general
municipal law relating to photo speed violation monitoring systems in
school speed zones in the city of New York, in relation to the effec-
tiveness thereof; and the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to estab-
lishing photo speed violation monitoring systems on the long island
expressway

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

Allows for an officer-operated hand-held photo speed enforcement tech-
nology pilot program in NYC as well as Nassau and Suffolk Counties

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

§ 1. Amends the existing NYC school zone program for three additional
years.

§ 2. Amends section 1180-C of the Vehicle and Traffic Law:
*by adding the Long Island Expressway (LIE) to the demonstration program
*Imposes monetary liability for failure to operate within the legal
speed limit.
*Defines the parameters for the pilot programming including access to
the photographs and retention time
*Defining the necessary calibration of these devices training of the
users.
*Defines what is an eligible device
*Lays out procedure for the notification of violators.
*Requires a report to the legislature on the effectiveness of the
program

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Our policies cannot merely police speeding after the damage is done -
our law enforcement must deter speeding from the get-go, and address the
"taboo" solution:

photo speed enforcement. The New York Daily News reported, "authorities
and witnesses of the deadly crash said that the car ...  was speeding
before it veered across a divider into oncoming traffic on the LIE." The
car "went flying." It struck two vehicles on its way down. The high
death toll also overshadows the EIGHT injuries that also occurred after
this horrific crash. http://www.nydailyne ws.com/newyor k/sixth-vict
im-dies-crash -ong-island-ex pressway-article-1.2761511 http://pixii.c
om/2016/08/2 1/three-de ad-several-injured -after-multi-vehic le-cra-
shon-lie/. This driving behavior is unfortunately not uncommon and
should not be normalized
  The  death toll on the LIE was so horrific, that even those who called
for repealing the school zone cameras are begging for speed  cameras  on
the LIE. Nassau County Comptroller says it has been the "worst in memory
in  deaths  on  the  LIE" in an interview on News 12. Comptroller George
Maragos even made a statement on Twitter: "Perhaps speed cameras on  the
LIE?" The fact a public official is calling for speed cameras on the LIE
shows that his constituents are on board as well. Maragos stated what we
believe  to  be true - that the speed cameras have been proven effective

to save lives. http://lo ngisland.news12. com/n ews/nassau-officia lsug-
gests-lie-sp eed-cameras-to-cu rb-crashes-1.12262627

In  light  of  recent  events  on the Long Island Expressway ("LIE") and
other highways, it  is  necessary  to  implement  This  technology  uses
throughout  Long  Island  and on the LIE. This would not be inconsistent
with current enforcement of speed and traffic laws  on  said  roads  and
highways, as This technology is analogous to the commonly-used and wide-
ly-accepted evidence from the radar/LIDAR guns.

It  is  necessary  to use improvements in existing technology to enhance
safety, efficiency and our lifestyle. It is an unfortunate reality  that
most  drivers speed on all roads, often leading to other infractions and
violations as well (weaving in and out of cars, etc.). Our laws and  law
enforcement  must evolve at the same pace as technology - or at the very
least, try to match the exponential growth of technology in  our  lives.
The  current  scheme  to  enforce speeding violations is technologically
limited - it is categorically impossible for a police officer to capture
an accurate proportion of lawbreakers as they speed down a road, and  it
is  often time consuming for an officer to make even one stop. The Tech-
nology available is the perfect compromise to  promote  officer  safety,
capture  more  drivers  who  violate  our necessary (not optional) speed
laws, and deter dangerous and disastrous driving behaviors; it  includes
participation  by law enforcement officers, and accomplishes the endeav-
ors of current "photo speed  violation  monitoring  systems"  -  without
using  fixed  technology  and  without  automatically issuing tickets to
unsuspecting drivers.

These lives also include the lives of our law enforcement officials.  It
is inherently dangerous for a police officer to pull out at  go  MPH  to
chase  after  a  speeding vehicle - and confront an unknown, potentially
dangerous offender. It is also inherently dangerous to stand alongside a
pulled over car and risk being hit. Police officers would no longer face
this risk every time a speeding ticket would be issued,  thanks  to  the
new technology.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New legislation

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

Minor if any if they choose to opt in

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This  act  shall  take  effect  immediately; provided, however, that the
amendments to section 1180-c of the vehicle  and  traffic  law  made  by
section  two  of this act shall not affect the expiation of such section
and shall be deemed repealed therewith.

summary: Establishes photo speed violation monitoring systems on the Long Island expressway; extends certain photo speed violation monitoring systems in Suffolk and Nassau counties.
